stem: What does a Prometheus client library do when Prometheus scrapes your application?

options.text: Sends the current state of all tracked metrics over HTTP
options.note: Right. The library serves the current values of every registered metric.

options.text: Pushes every individual event to Prometheus as it happens
options.note: Client libraries hold aggregated values, such as counter totals, and serve them on request. They don't stream events.

options.text: Writes metrics to a log file for Prometheus to read
options.note: Prometheus scrapes an HTTP endpoint. It doesn't read log files.

options.text: Queries the Prometheus server for alert rules
options.note: That's not what client libraries do.

explanation: When Prometheus scrapes your instance's HTTP endpoint, the client library sends the current state of all tracked metrics to the server.
hint: Pull model: what's in the response to a scrape?

stem: Which of these are official Prometheus client libraries? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. client_golang is official.
Right. client_python is official.
Right. client_java is official.
PHP is listed under unofficial third-party libraries.

explanation: Official libraries: Go, Java or Scala, Node.js, Python, Ruby and Rust. PHP, C++, .NET and others are third-party.
hint: One of these is listed among the third-party libraries.

stem: There is no client library for your language. What do the docs suggest?

options.text: Implement one of the supported exposition formats yourself
options.note: Right. The text format is simple enough to write by hand.

options.text: You can't monitor that application with Prometheus
options.note: You can. Expose the format yourself, or use an exporter.
The Pushgateway is for batch jobs, not a replacement for exposing metrics.

options.text: Write metrics to a database Prometheus reads
options.note: Prometheus doesn't read from arbitrary databases.

explanation: If no client library is available for your language, or you want to avoid dependencies, you may implement one of the supported exposition formats yourself.
hint: Think back to the exposition format topic.

stem: In a client library, what happens if you call inc(-5) on a counter?

options.text: It's rejected, because counter increments must be ≥ 0
options.note: Right. Libraries must check that v ≥ 0, since counters never decrease.
Counters must never decrease.
A reset only happens on restart, not through a negative increment.
There's no silent conversion. Negative values are rejected.

explanation: A counter must have inc() and inc(double v), and the library must check that v ≥ 0. Counters must not allow the value to decrease.
hint: What's the defining rule of a counter?

stem: Which methods must a client library gauge provide? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. Gauges can go up.
Right. Gauges can go down.
Right. Gauges can be set to any value.
observe() belongs to summaries and histograms.

explanation: A gauge must have inc(), inc(v), dec(), dec(v) and set(v), and should have set_to_current_time().
hint: Gauges go up, down, or to a value. Which method records an observation instead?

stem: Which gauge method is handy for a batch job's "last success" metric?

options.note: Right. It sets the gauge to the current Unix time in seconds, a timestamp metric.
Incrementing doesn't record when something happened.
Gauges don't have observe(). That's for summaries and histograms.
labels() selects a child series. It doesn't set a time.

explanation: A gauge should have set_to_current_time(), which sets it to the current Unix time in seconds, which fits the timestamps-not-time-since practice.
hint: You want the time of the last success.

stem: By default, what does a client library summary expose?

options.note: Right. Quantiles must be optional, and no quantiles is the default.
Quantiles are optional. By default a summary only has _count and _sum.
Buckets are histograms.
_count and _sum are useful by themselves and are exposed by default.

explanation: A summary must allow having no quantiles, since _count and _sum alone are useful, and this must be the default. Quantiles can't be aggregated and tend to be slow.
hint: The guidelines say the two basic series are useful on their own.

stem: Which user-set label names must client libraries forbid? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. le is used internally for buckets.
Right. quantile is used internally for summary quantiles.
method is a perfectly normal label name.
Libraries don't forbid it outright, though Prometheus sets job at scrape time.

explanation: A histogram must not allow le as a user-set label, and a summary must not allow quantile, because these designate buckets and quantiles internally.
hint: Which label names did histograms and summaries use in the exposition format?

stem: Your code creates metrics named requests_total_user_42, requests_total_user_43 and so on. What do the client library guidelines say?

options.text: Generated metric names are a sign you should be using labels instead
options.note: Right. Better still, avoid unbounded values such as user IDs entirely.

options.text: This is the recommended way to track per-user data
options.note: Dynamic names are explicitly discouraged.

options.text: It's fine as long as each name has a help string
options.note: Help strings don't fix the naming problem.

options.text: Client libraries automatically convert them into labels
options.note: Libraries don't do that conversion.

explanation: Dynamic or generated metric names must be discouraged, except when proxying from other systems. They're a sign you should be using labels instead.

stem: Which metrics do client libraries typically export by default without any work from you? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. A standard process metric.
Right. A standard process metric.
Right. A standard process metric (a timestamp).
Request counts are application-specific. You add them yourself.

explanation: Client libraries should offer the standard process metrics (prefix process_) registered by default, plus runtime metrics such as go_*.
hint: Which ones describe the process itself rather than your application's work?

stem: How do you increment a labelled counter for method="GET" and code="200" in a typical client library?

options.text: Call labels("GET", "200") to get a child, then call inc() on it
options.note: Right. labels() returns a child for that label combination, which you can cache.

options.text: Create a new metric named requests_GET_200
options.note: That's the dynamic naming the guidelines discourage.
inc() takes an optional amount, not label values.

options.text: Labels can only be added by Prometheus at scrape time
options.note: Instrumented code can define its own labels.

explanation: The general way to access a labelled dimension is a labels() method that returns a child, on which you call .inc(), .dec() or .observe(). The child should be cacheable.
hint: Labels select a child series first.
